question_text: An 11-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of severe abdominal pain. She says that the pain started near the middle of her abdomen and moved to the right lower quadrant after about 10 hours. Several hours after the pain started she also started experiencing nausea and loss of appetite. On presentation, her temperature is 102.5°F (39.2°C), blood pressure is 115/74 mmHg, pulse is 102/min, and respirations are 21/min. Physical exam reveals rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Raising the patient's right leg with the knee flexed significantly increases the pain. Which of the following is the most common cause of this patient's symptoms in children?

                    ### Question
                    An 11-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of severe abdominal pain. She says that the pain started near the middle of her abdomen and moved to the right lower quadrant after about 10 hours. Several hours after the pain started she also started experiencing nausea and loss of appetite. On presentation, her temperature is 102.5°F (39.2°C), blood pressure is 115/74 mmHg, pulse is 102/min, and respirations are 21/min. Physical exam reveals rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Raising the patient's right leg with the knee flexed significantly increases the pain. Which of the following is the most common cause of this patient's symptoms in children?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Fecalith obstruction
opb. Ingestion of indigestible object
opc. Lymphoid hyperplasia
opd. Meckel diverticulum
ope. Parasitic infection

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of severe abdominal pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, accompanied by rebound tenderness, fever, and nausea, strongly suggests appendicitis. The most common cause of appendicitis in children is fecalith obstruction, which is supported by the reasoning chains indicating that obstruction leads to inflammation. While lymphoid hyperplasia can also cause appendicitis, it is less common than fecalith obstruction in this age group. Therefore, the consensus aligns with the conclusion that fecalith obstruction is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms.
